items.description: Ceres — Roman goddess of agriculture, holding wheat and sickle

items.motif: Aristides Lobo (1839-1896) — lawyer, politician, journalist, republican abolitionist, with Liberty allegorical frame
items.description: Aristides Lobo (1839-1896) — lawyer, politician, journalist, republican abolitionist, with Liberty allegorical frame
items.notes: Old Republic (República Velha) period. Portrait flanked by allegorical Liberty frame, linking republican founding figures to classical iconography.

items.motif: Benjamin Constant (1833-1891) — author, poet, politician, with Liberty allegorical frame
items.description: Benjamin Constant (1833-1891) — author, poet, politician, with Liberty allegorical frame
items.notes: Benjamin Constant Botelho de Magalhães, founder of the Brazilian Republic (proclaimed 1889). Liberty allegory framing device in the stamp design.

items.motif: Deodoro da Fonseca (1827-1892) — first President of Brazil, with Liberty allegorical frame
items.description: Deodoro da Fonseca (1827-1892) — first President of Brazil, with Liberty allegorical frame
items.notes: Marshal Deodoro da Fonseca, proclaimed the Republic on 15 November 1889. The Liberty allegorical frame synthesizes republican founding figure + classical icon.

items.motif: Liberty Allegory — seated female figure of Liberty with shield and wreath
items.description: Liberty Allegory — seated female figure of Liberty with shield and wreath
items.notes: High-value definitive showing the full Liberty allegory without a portrait. Seated female Liberty with shield, a classic republican iconographic motif.

items.motif: Allegory of the Republic — female Republic figure with instructions tablet
items.description: Allegory of the Republic — female Republic figure with instructions tablet
items.series: Allegory of the Republic and Instructions
items.notes: Female Republic personification holding a tablet inscribed with instructions — a didactic iconocratic device fusing allegory and civic pedagogy.

items.motif: Allegory of Liberty Seated — seated female Liberty with shield and coat of arms
items.description: Allegory of Liberty Seated — seated female Liberty with shield and coat of arms
items.designer: unknown (engraved by Waterlow & Sons or Compañía Sudamericana de Billetes de Banco)
items.notes: First issued ~1892, re-engraved 1899. Perf 11½. Classic seated Liberty, a motif shared across Latin American republican philately.

items.motif: Allegory of Liberty Seated — seated female Liberty with shield and coat of arms (perf 11½x12¼ variant)
items.description: Allegory of Liberty Seated — seated female Liberty with shield and coat of arms (perf 11½x12¼ variant)
items.notes: Perforation variant (11½x12¼). Minor variant of the main Liberty Seated type.

items.motif: Allegory of Liberty Seated — seated female Liberty with shield and coat of arms (perf 12¼ variant)
items.description: Allegory of Liberty Seated — seated female Liberty with shield and coat of arms (perf 12¼ variant)
items.notes: Perforation variant (12¼). 2c denomination.

items.motif: Lady Justice — seated female figure with scales and sword, allegory of Justice
items.description: Lady Justice — seated female figure with scales and sword, allegory of Justice
items.notes: Post-civil war constitutional period (Batllism). Justice allegory common in Latin American definitive series of the late 19th century.

items.motif: Germania — female personification of Germany, wearing octagonal imperial crown, holding sword and olive branch
items.description: Germania — female personification of Germany, wearing octagonal imperial crown, holding sword and olive branch. First issue with REICHSPOST inscription.
items.designer: Paul Eduard Waldraff (engraver), model: actress Anna Führing
items.notes: First Germania definitive issue. Inscribed REICHSPOST. The octagonal imperial crown and martial attributes (sword) encode Wilhelmine imperial ideology. The olive branch adds a pacific counter-note.

items.motif: Germania — female personification of Germany, wearing octagonal imperial crown, holding sword and olive branch
items.description: Germania — female personification of Germany, wearing octagonal imperial crown, holding sword and olive branch. Inscription changed to DEUTSCHES REICH.
items.designer: Paul Eduard Waldraff (engraver), model: actress Anna Führing
items.notes: Inscription changed from REICHSPOST to DEUTSCHES REICH. The Germania motif consolidated as the iconographic face of the German Empire's postal system.

items.motif: Germania — female personification of Germany, wearing octagonal imperial crown, holding sword and olive branch
items.description: Germania — peace-issue Germania, DEUTSCHES REICH inscription. Carmine-rose.
items.designer: Paul Eduard Waldraff (engraver), model: actress Anna Führing
items.series: Germania Definitives — DEUTSCHES REICH peace issues
items.notes: Peace-issue definitive. Used throughout the Empire for domestic postage. 10pf carmine-rose was one of the most common Germania stamps in circulation.

items.motif: Germania — female personification of Germany, wearing octagonal imperial crown, holding sword and olive branch
items.description: Germania — DEUTSCHES REICH, peace-issue definitive. Ultramarine.
items.designer: Paul Eduard Waldraff (engraver), model: actress Anna Führing
items.series: Germania Definitives — DEUTSCHES REICH peace issues
items.notes: 20pf peace-issue definitive. Ultramarine. Ubiquitous in late Wilhelmine postal traffic.

items.motif: Germania — female personification of Germany, war printing on lower-quality paper
items.description: Germania — war printing (Kriegsdruck). Lower-quality paper, coarser gum, simplified printing due to wartime material shortages.
items.designer: Paul Eduard Waldraff (engraver), model: actress Anna Führing
items.notes: WWI war printing (Kriegsdruck). 3pf brown. Paper quality degraded due to British naval blockade. The Germania image persists as wartime propaganda icon.

items.motif: Germania — female personification of Germany, war printing
items.description: Germania — war printing (Kriegsdruck). Mid-WWI issue adapting to wartime postal rates.
items.designer: Paul Eduard Waldraff (engraver), model: actress Anna Führing
items.notes: 15pf war printing. New denomination introduced during WWI to meet changing postal rates.

items.motif: Germania — female personification of Germany, late-war printing
items.description: Germania — late WWI war printing. Darker colors, rougher paper. DEUTSCHES REICH inscription.
items.designer: Paul Eduard Waldraff (engraver), model: actress Anna Führing
items.notes: Late-war printing, 1917. Increasing material degradation visible in paper and gum. Germania endures as the Empire's last philatelic icon before collapse in November 1918.

items.motif: Germania — female personification of Germany, overprinted for the Weimar Republic
items.description: Germania definitive with Weimar Republic overprint. Surviving imperial Germania stock repurposed by the new republican government.
items.designer: Paul Eduard Waldraff (engraver), model: actress Anna Führing
items.notes: Post-WWI transition. Imperial Germania stamps overprinted for the Weimar Republic — a palimpsest of collapsing empire and emerging democracy. The icon remains but the regime inscription shifted.

items.motif: Germania — female personification of Germany, plebiscite overprint for Allenstein
items.description: Germania definitive overprinted for the Allenstein plebiscite territory (East Prussia). The Germania figure used as a national identity marker in disputed borderlands.
items.designer: Paul Eduard Waldraff (engraver), model: actress Anna Führing
items.notes: Allenstein (Olsztyn) plebiscite territory, 1920. Germania stamps overprinted as instruments of national self-determination in post-Versailles border referenda. The allegorical female figure functions as a territorial claim.

items.motif: Germania — female personification of Germany, high-inflation definitive
items.description: Germania definitive at hyperinflation value. 5 Mark denomination reflects the collapsing currency of early Weimar Germany.
items.designer: Paul Eduard Waldraff (engraver), model: actress Anna Führing
items.series: Germania Definitives — Weimar overprints / high inflation (1919–1922)
items.notes: 5 Mark denomination at the onset of hyperinflation (1922–1923). The last Germania issues before the motif was retired. The same female allegory that inaugurated the Empire in 1900 now marks its terminal economic crisis.

items.motif: Marianne — female personification of the French Republic, wearing Phrygian cap
items.description: Marianne — allegorical female figure representing Liberty and the French Republic. Wearing a Phrygian cap (bonnet phrygien), a republican symbol dating to the Revolution.
items.notes: Third Republic (1870–1940). The Morlon Marianne circulated through the interwar period, the Popular Front, and into the Vichy regime (until replaced). Aluminum-bronze. Marianne is the most enduring icon of French republicanism.

items.motif: Britannia — seated female personification of Britain, holding trident and shield with Union Jack
items.description: Britannia — classical female personification of Great Britain. Seated, holding trident (maritime power) and shield bearing the Union Jack. Obverse: Victoria 'Bun Head' portrait.
items.designer: Leonard Charles Wyon (reverse: Britannia), William Wyon (obverse: Victoria)
items.notes: Bronze penny. Britannia type introduced 1860 replacing the earlier copper coinage. A rare case of a female allegory (Britannia) coexisting with a female monarch (Victoria) on the same coin.

items.motif: Hispania — reclining female personification of Spain, with Pyrenees mountains at her feet, holding olive branch
items.description: Hispania — reclining female allegory of Spain. Holding an olive branch, with the Pyrenees mountains at her feet. Obverse: personification of the Spanish Republic emerging after the Glorious Revolution.
items.notes: Issued by the Provisional Government after the 1868 Glorious Revolution (La Gloriosa) that deposed Isabel II. The reclining Hispania with the Pyrenees was the first coin of the Spanish peseta system and a foundational republican icon.

items.motif: Hispania — seated female personification of Spain, holding olive branch, with coat of arms
items.description: Seated Hispania — female allegory of the Second Spanish Republic. Seated, holding an olive branch. The coat of arms of the Republic appears beside her.
items.notes: Second Spanish Republic coinage. Silver (.835). The seated Hispania replaced the monarchical portrait, marking a deliberate republican iconographic break. Issued during the reformist biennium (1931–1933) and conservative biennium (1933–1936).

items.motif: Female head personifying the Republic — allegorical bust with Phrygian cap or classical coiffure
items.description: Female head of the Republic (Rubia type) — allegorical bust representing the Spanish Republic. Issued by the Nationalist side during the Civil War.
items.notes: Issued 1937 by the Francoist (Nationalist) side during the Civil War. Brass (latón). Paradoxically, the Nationalists appropriated the female Republic allegory on their coinage while fighting against the Republic — an iconocratic contradiction.

items.motif: Marianne — female personification of the French Republic, wearing Phrygian cap
items.description: Marianne type Blanc — allegorical female figure representing Liberty and the French Republic. Wearing a Phrygian cap (bonnet phrygien). 5c green. First issue of the Blanc type.
items.notes: Third Republic period. The Blanc Marianne inaugurated the modern definitive series tradition in France. The Phrygian cap echoes the sans-culottes of the 1789 Revolution, making this a direct iconographic link to republican origins.

items.motif: Marianne — female personification of the French Republic, wearing Phrygian cap
items.description: Marianne type Blanc — allegorical female figure representing Liberty and the French Republic. 10c red.
items.notes: Third Republic period. Same Blanc design as 5c, different denomination and color.

items.motif: Marianne — female personification of the French Republic, wearing Phrygian cap
items.description: Marianne type Blanc — allegorical female figure representing Liberty and the French Republic. 15c blue.
items.notes: Third Republic period. Same Blanc design, higher denomination.

items.motif: Marianne — female personification of the French Republic, wearing Phrygian cap
items.description: Marianne type Gandon — allegorical female figure representing the French Republic. 6F red. Post-WWII definitive series of the Fourth Republic.
items.notes: Fourth Republic (1946–1958). Gandon's Marianne was the first new definitive after Liberation. The Phrygian cap re-emerges after the Vichy interregnum, reasserting republican legitimacy.

items.motif: Marianne — female personification of the French Republic, wearing Phrygian cap
items.description: Marianne type Gandon — allegorical female figure representing the French Republic. 12F green.
items.notes: Fourth Republic. Gandon type, 12F denomination.

items.motif: Marianne — female personification of the French Republic, wearing Phrygian cap
items.description: Marianne type Gandon — allegorical female figure representing the French Republic. 18F blue.
items.notes: Fourth Republic. Gandon type, 18F high denomination.

items.motif: Marianne — female personification of the French Republic, wearing Phrygian cap
items.description: Marianne de Cheffer — allegorical female figure representing the French Republic. 0.25F green. Fifth Republic definitive.
items.notes: Fifth Republic (1958–), early Gaullist period. Cheffer's Marianne presents a more stylized, modern profile while retaining the Phrygian cap.

items.motif: Marianne — female personification of the French Republic, wearing Phrygian cap
items.description: Marianne de Cheffer — allegorical female figure representing the French Republic. 0.40F red.
items.notes: Fifth Republic. Cheffer type, 0.40F denomination.

items.motif: Marianne — female personification of the French Republic, bicentennial of Revolution
items.description: Marianne de Briat — allegorical female figure representing the French Republic. 2.30F green. Issued for the bicentennial of the French Revolution.
items.notes: Issued during the 1989 bicentennial of the French Revolution. Briat's Marianne reinterprets the allegory in a contemporary, almost abstract style, connecting the Revolution's legacy to the late Fifth Republic under Mitterrand.

items.motif: Marianne — female personification of the French Republic, bicentennial of Revolution
items.description: Marianne de Briat — allegorical female figure representing the French Republic. 2.50F red.
items.notes: Bicentennial Marianne. Briat type, 2.50F denomination.

items.motif: Marianne — female personification of the French Republic, wearing Phrygian cap
items.description: Marianne de Lamouche — allegorical female figure representing the French Republic. 0.53€ green. First Marianne series denominated in euros.
items.notes: Euro-denominated Marianne. Lamouche's design signals the French Republic's continuity through the currency transition from franc to euro. The Phrygian cap persists as the unchanging republican signifier.

items.motif: Marianne — female personification of the French Republic, wearing Phrygian cap
items.description: Marianne de Lamouche — allegorical female figure representing the French Republic. 0.55€ red.
items.notes: Lamouche type, 0.55€ denomination.

items.motif: Marianne — female personification of the French Republic, wearing Phrygian cap
items.description: Marianne de Beaujard — allegorical female figure representing the French Republic. 0.55€ red. The Marianne of the Sarkozy presidency.
items.notes: Beaujard's Marianne (also known as 'Marianne de Beaujard' or 'Marianne de l'Europe') was selected by President Sarkozy. The design includes European stars, linking the national allegory to EU identity.

items.motif: Marianne — female personification of the French Republic, wearing Phrygian cap
items.description: Marianne de Beaujard — allegorical female figure representing the French Republic. 0.70€ green.
items.notes: Beaujard type, 0.70€ denomination.

items.motif: Semeuse (Sower) — female personification of agricultural France, sowing seeds at sunrise
items.description: Semeuse type Blanc — the Sower, a female allegory of agricultural France and republican fertility. 15c green. Walking woman scattering seeds against the rising sun.
items.notes: The Semeuse is one of the most iconic French stamp designs, adapted from Roty's 1897 Sower motif originally used on coins. The Sower merges agricultural imagery with republican allegory — a female figure 'sowing' the ideas of the Republic.

items.motif: Semeuse (Sower) — female personification of agricultural France, sowing seeds at sunrise
items.description: Semeuse type Blanc — the Sower, female allegory of agricultural France and republican fertility. 10c red.
items.notes: Semeuse type, 10c denomination.

items.motif: Semeuse (Sower) — female personification of agricultural France, sowing seeds at sunrise
items.description: Semeuse type Blanc — the Sower, female allegory of agricultural France and republican fertility. 20c purple.
items.notes: Semeuse type, 20c denomination.

items.motif: Semeuse (Sower) — female personification of agricultural France, sowing seeds at sunrise
items.description: Semeuse type Blanc — the Sower, female allegory of agricultural France and republican fertility. 25c blue.
items.notes: Semeuse type, 25c denomination.

items.motif: Helvetia — seated female personification of Switzerland, with Swiss shield and alpine landscape
items.description: Sitting Helvetia — female allegory of Switzerland, seated in classical toga with Swiss shield, against an alpine backdrop. 5Rp brown. First Helvetia definitive series.
items.notes: First federal definitive series after the 1848 Swiss Federal Constitution. Helvetia seated in a mountain setting links the female allegory to the national territory, encoding Swiss identity through landscape iconography.

items.motif: Helvetia — seated female personification of Switzerland, with Swiss shield and alpine landscape
items.description: Sitting Helvetia — female allegory of Switzerland. 10Rp blue.
items.notes: Sitting Helvetia series, 10Rp denomination.

items.motif: Helvetia — seated female personification of Switzerland, with Swiss shield and alpine landscape
items.description: Sitting Helvetia — female allegory of Switzerland. 1Fr gold. High-denomination definitive of the series.
items.notes: Sitting Helvetia series, 1Fr high denomination in gold. The 1881 date marks the consolidation of the federal postal system.

items.motif: Helvetia — standing female personification of Switzerland, holding spear and Swiss shield
items.description: Standing Helvetia — female allegory of Switzerland, standing with spear and Swiss shield. 5c green. New definitive series replacing the Sitting Helvetia.
items.notes: The Standing Helvetia marks an iconographic shift from the contemplative seated figure to an upright, martial stance — reflecting Switzerland's consolidated federal identity and military readiness.

items.motif: Helvetia — standing female personification of Switzerland, holding spear and Swiss shield
items.description: Standing Helvetia — female allegory of Switzerland, standing with spear and Swiss shield. 10c red.
items.notes: Standing Helvetia series, 10c denomination.

items.motif: Helvetia with sword — female personification of Switzerland in martial stance
items.description: Helvetia with sword — female allegory of Switzerland in an actively martial pose, holding a raised sword. 40c. Designed by L'Eplattenier.
items.notes: The martial Helvetia with raised sword is the most explicitly militarized version of the Swiss allegory. L'Eplattenier, a leading Swiss Art Nouveau artist, fused national iconography with Jugendstil aesthetics.

items.motif: Italia turrita — female personification of Italy, wearing turreted crown, with fasces
items.description: Imperial Series — Italia turrita, the female allegory of Italy crowned with a turreted crown (corona turrita), representing Italian cities and civilization. 15c. Fascist-era definitive with fasces (lictorial bundle) as state symbol.
items.notes: Fascist-era definitive ('Serie Imperiale'). Paschetto's design merges the classical Italia turrita motif with the fasces, the symbol of the Fascist regime. The turreted crown dates to Roman antiquity (Cybele/Magna Mater as protector of cities).

items.motif: Italia turrita — female personification of Italy, wearing turreted crown, with fasces
items.description: Imperial Series — Italia turrita, the female allegory of Italy crowned with a turreted crown. 20c. Fascist-era definitive.
items.notes: Imperial Series, 20c denomination. Same design as 15c.

items.motif: Italia turrita — female personification of Italy, with GNR (Guardia Nazionale Repubblicana) overprint
items.description: Italia turrita with GNR overprint — Imperial Series stamp overprinted for the Italian Social Republic (Repubblica Sociale Italiana, RSI). The female allegory persists through regime collapse and Nazi-backed puppet state.
items.designer: Paolo Paschetto (original), overprint by RSI postal authorities
items.notes: Italian Social Republic (RSI), the Nazi-backed puppet state in northern Italy (1943–1945). The GNR (Guardia Nazionale Repubblicana) overprint on the Imperial Series stamps shows the reuse of fascist-era iconography by the Salò regime. Italia turrita becomes a contested symbol between the Kingdom, the RSI, and the Resistance.

items.motif: Italia turrita — female personification of Italy, wearing turreted crown, without fasces
items.description: Italia turrita without fasces — post-war republican definitive. The turreted crown remains, but the fascist fasces has been removed. The same allegorical female figure now serves the Italian Republic.
items.notes: Post-war Italian Republic (established 1946). The removal of the fasces from the Italia turrita design is a precise act of iconoclastic purification — the same allegorical female body is stripped of regime-specific symbols and repurposed for democratic republicanism.

items.motif: Germania — female personification of Germany, wearing octagonal imperial crown, holding sword and olive branch
items.description: Germania REICHSPOST definitive. 3pf brown. First issue of the Germania series, pre-dating the DEUTSCHES REICH inscription change.
items.designer: Paul Eduard Waldraff (engraver), model: actress Anna Führing
items.notes: REICHSPOST-inscribed Germania. 3pf brown, one of the earliest denominations in the series. The octagonal imperial crown (Reichskrone) is a central iconographic element marking Wilhelmine imperial authority.

items.motif: Germania — female personification of Germany, wearing octagonal imperial crown, holding sword and olive branch
items.description: Germania REICHSPOST definitive. 5pf green.
items.designer: Paul Eduard Waldraff (engraver), model: actress Anna Führing
items.notes: REICHSPOST-inscribed Germania, 5pf green.

items.motif: Germania — female personification of Germany, wearing octagonal imperial crown, holding sword and olive branch
items.description: Germania DEUTSCHES REICH definitive. 2pf grey. Inscription changed from REICHSPOST to DEUTSCHES REICH in 1902.
items.designer: Paul Eduard Waldraff (engraver), model: actress Anna Führing
items.notes: DEUTSCHES REICH inscription. The change from REICHSPOST to DEUTSCHES REICH reflects the consolidation of imperial identity — the postal service becomes an instrument of national rather than merely administrative branding.

items.motif: Germania — female personification of Germany, war printing on degraded paper
items.description: Germania war printing (Kriegsdruck). 15pf brown-red. WWI-era issue on lower-quality paper due to British naval blockade material shortages.
items.designer: Paul Eduard Waldraff (engraver), model: actress Anna Führing
items.notes: WWI war printing. 15pf brown-red. The degradation of paper quality mirrors the deteriorating material conditions of the German war effort. Germania as propaganda icon endures even as the physical medium crumbles.

items.motif: Germania — female personification of Germany, overprinted for the Free State of Bavaria
items.description: Germania overprinted 'Freistaat Bayern' — imperial Germania stock repurposed by the revolutionary Bavarian Free State after the fall of the Wittelsbach monarchy.
items.designer: Paul Eduard Waldraff (engraver), model: actress Anna Führing
items.notes: Overprinted for the Free State of Bavaria (Freistaat Bayern), proclaimed November 1918 after the abdication of King Ludwig III. The Germania figure, originally an imperial icon, is repurposed by a revolutionary republican government — an iconocratic palimpsest.

items.motif: Germania — female personification of Germany, overprinted for the Saar territory
items.description: Germania overprinted 'Saargebiet' — imperial Germania stock overprinted for the Saar territory under League of Nations mandate after the Treaty of Versailles.
items.designer: Paul Eduard Waldraff (engraver), model: actress Anna Führing
items.notes: Saargebiet (Saar Territory) overprint. The Saar was placed under League of Nations administration for 15 years. The Germania figure, overprinted with a foreign administrative mark, becomes a territorial claim frozen in philatelic form — the allegorical body claims what political borders contest.

items.motif: Germania — female personification of Germany, overprinted for the Free City of Danzig
items.description: Germania overprinted 'Danzig' — imperial Germania stock overprinted for the Free City of Danzig, established as a semi-autonomous city-state under League of Nations protection.
items.designer: Paul Eduard Waldraff (engraver), model: actress Anna Führing
items.notes: Danzig (Gdańsk) overprint. The Free City was created by the Treaty of Versailles as a compromise between German and Polish claims. The Germania overprint transforms a national allegory into a contested territorial marker at one of the 20th century's most disputed borderlands.

items.motif: Allegory of Justice — seated woman holding scales and sword
items.description: Allegory of Justice — seated woman holding scales and sword. 25c blue. Part of the Allegory of Justice series.
items.notes: Allegory of Justice series. 25c denomination. Issued under Alfonso XII (constitutional monarchy). The series combines classical allegorical iconography with Bourbon restoration state-building through philately.

items.motif: Allegory of the Republic — female personification of the Spanish Republic
items.description: Allegory of the Republic — female personification of the Spanish Republic. 30c red. Issued by the Republican side during the Spanish Civil War.
items.notes: Republican stamp issued during the Spanish Civil War (1936–1939). The female Republic allegory served as a mobilizing icon for the Republican cause against the Francoist Nationalists. Issued in the war's final year, with Republican defeat imminent.

items.motif: Liberty Allegory — seated female figure of Liberty with shield and wreath
items.description: Liberty Allegory — seated female Liberty with shield and wreath. 50 réis. Standalone Liberty allegory stamp from the Personalities and Liberty Allegory series.
items.notes: Old Republic (República Velha) period. The seated Liberty allegory without a portrait frames the abstract Republic as a standalone icon, distinct from the personality-plus-frame format of the lower denominations in the same series.

items.motif: Liberty Allegory — seated female figure of Liberty with shield and wreath
items.description: Liberty Allegory — seated female Liberty with shield and wreath. 100 réis. Higher-denomination Liberty allegory stamp.
items.notes: Old Republic period. 100 réis Liberty allegory. The higher-value stamps in the series carried the full allegorical figure, suggesting that higher postal denominations carried greater iconocratic weight.

items.motif: Effigy of the Republic — female profile looking left, personifying the Brazilian Republic
items.description: Effigy of the Republic — female personification of the Brazilian Republic in profile, looking left. 1 Cruzeiro note, 147×66mm. The model for the Republic effigy was actress Tonia Carrero.
items.notes: Issued during the Brazilian military dictatorship (1964–1985). The Republic effigy modelled on Tonia Carrero, a renowned Brazilian actress, is a notable case of the female allegory being modelled on a living cultural figure. Designer Aloísio Magalhães was a major figure in Brazilian graphic design.

items.motif: Effigy of the Republic — female profile (Liberty) as watermark, with Proclamation of Republic scene
items.description: Effigy of the Republic — Liberty in profile as central watermark. Reverse: painting of the Proclamation of the Republic (1889). 200 Cruzeiros, 140×65mm.
items.notes: Post-dictatorship period, issued shortly after the 1988 Constitution (the 'Citizen Constitution'). The Republic effigy paired with the Proclamation of 1889 scene links the new democratic era to its republican founding moment. Part of the currency transition during hyperinflation.

items.motif: Germania — female personification of Germany, with child and dove of peace
items.description: Germania with child and dove — female allegory of Germany holding a child in her arms, with a dove symbolizing peace. 5 Mark Reichskassenschein (Imperial Treasury Note). 125×80mm, intaglio printing on hemp paper.
items.notes: Reichskassenschein (Imperial Treasury Note), distinct from Reichsbanknote. The Germania-with-child motif adds a maternal dimension to the martial Germania of the stamps — the allegorical female body serves both as warrior (on stamps) and mother (on banknotes). Alexander Zick was a noted German historical and genre painter.

items.motif: Italia turrita — female personification of Italy, wearing turreted crown
items.description: Italia turrita — female allegory of Italy with turreted crown. 100 Lire, Bank of Italy, WWII issue under Vittorio Emanuele III. 135×60mm.
items.notes: WWII-era banknote issued while Italy was split between the Allied-occupied south (Kingdom of Italy) and the German-occupied north (Italian Social Republic). Italia turrita on wartime paper money shows the allegorical female figure functioning as a claim to legitimate statehood amid civil war and foreign occupation.

items.motif: Helvetia seated — female personification of Switzerland in toga, seated in alpine landscape with Swiss shield
items.description: Helvetia seated — female allegory of Switzerland. Seated in classical toga against a mountain backdrop, holding a spear with Swiss shield beside her. Silver .900, 2.5g, 18.2mm. First federal coinage of Switzerland.
items.notes: First federal coinage after the 1848 Swiss Federal Constitution. The seated Helvetia in an alpine setting is the foundational icon of Swiss federal identity, replacing the patchwork of cantonal coinages. The toga links Helvetia to classical republican iconography.

items.motif: Helvetia standing — full-length female personification of Switzerland, with spear and shield, 22 stars
items.description: Helvetia standing — full-length female allegory of Switzerland. Standing with spear and Swiss shield, surrounded by 22 stars representing the cantons. Silver .835, 5g, 23.3mm. 92-year minting run.
items.notes: 92-year run (1875–1967), one of the longest-running coin designs in modern numismatic history. Demonetized in 1971 — the same year Swiss women gained the federal vote. The 22 stars encode the federal structure, making each coin a miniature constitutional diagram.

items.motif: Italia turrita — female head personification of Italy, wearing turreted crown
items.description: Italia turrita — female head of the Italian Republic, wearing the turreted crown (corona turrita). REPVBBLICA ITALIANA inscription. Acmonital, 22mm. One of the last lira coins before the euro.
items.notes: One of the last Italian lira coins before the euro replaced the lira in 2002. The Italia turrita, an icon stretching from Roman antiquity through the Risorgimento, Fascism, and the Republic, makes its final numismatic appearance on the 100 lire — a terminus to over a century of the turreted allegory on Italian coinage.
